analysis.one_liner: Lets each state cap the interest rates and fees lenders can charge its residents.
analysis.headline: A bill to let states cap credit card and consumer loan rates died in the Senate Banking Committee without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Under long-standing federal rules, a national bank can issue loans and credit cards nationwide using the interest rate of the state where it is chartered, no matter how strict the borrower's home state is. This bill would amend the Truth in Lending Act so that, with an exception for home mortgages, no consumer loan could carry an annual percentage rate—including fees—higher than the cap set by the state where the consumer lives. States that want to ban rates above, say, 36% could enforce those caps against every lender, not just in-state ones.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers who live in states with strict interest rate caps, especially borrowers who today get high-rate payday loans, installment loans, or high-APR credit cards from out-of-state banks.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Borrowers in states with rate caps

how_it_helps.text: The bill amends the Truth in Lending Act so the APR on any consumer credit transaction, including associated fees, may not exceed the maximum rate permitted by the laws of the state where the consumer resides [S2][S3].

It covers all consumer credit except residential mortgages, so it reaches credit cards, payday loans, and other installment lending, and it counts fees toward the cap so lenders cannot recoup charges through side fees [S3].
It applies 'notwithstanding any other provision of law,' which would override the federal rule that lets banks export the interest rate of their home state into every other state [S3].

analysis.who_pays: High-rate consumer lenders—credit card issuers, payday and installment lenders, and national banks whose business model relies on charging rates above what many states allow. Borrowers who are turned down because lenders can no longer price for their risk may lose access to some credit.

drawbacks.text: Lenders would face up to 50 different state rate regimes instead of one national one, which could mean less credit available and higher rates for some borrowers if lenders decline to lend in capped states or price for added compliance risk.
States with no meaningful rate cap would see no change, so the bill's protections would be uneven and depend entirely on each state legislature acting to set a cap.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For people in states with strict rate caps, the bill removes the federal loophole that makes those caps largely unenforceable against out-of-state banks, a real gain for low-income borrowers facing triple-digit APRs. The trade-off is that some risky borrowers may be denied credit altogether, and states without caps would get nothing. On balance, the bill shifts power over loan pricing from national banks to state legislatures.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Banking Committee on the day it was introduced and sat there until the Congress ended—no hearing, no markup, no floor vote.

narrative.text: Senator Sheldon Whitehouse introduced the bill on November 8, 2011, with seven Democratic cosponsors and one Independent, Senator Sanders [S4][S5].

The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs the same day; the committee took no further action before the 112th Congress ended in January 2013 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The national banking and consumer lending industry is better off, because the current rule letting banks charge any state's highest allowable rate nationwide remained untouched.

for.name: Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to let states cap APRs and spoke for it at introduction.

for.name: 8 senators
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill on the day it was introduced.

against.name: Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill—no hearing, no markup, no vote—before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All nine sponsors were Democrats or Independents; no Republican cosponsor appears in the record, and the bill never advanced past committee referral [S4][S5].

industries.industry: Consumer lending (payday, installment, and high-APR credit cards)
industries.note: The bill would let borrowers' home states cap the APR, including fees, that these lenders can charge, ending the practice of exporting high out-of-state rates nationwide. Their revenue comes directly from charging rates above what many states allow.

industries.industry: National banks and credit card issuers
industries.note: Many large card issuers charter in states with no rate cap (such as South Dakota and Delaware) and apply those rates to customers everywhere; the bill would subject them to each cardholder's home state cap.
